questions.prompt: What is collection mainly trying to do in Chapter 5?
choices: Gather loose incompletes into a trusted capture path
Rank every task by urgency immediately
Throw away anything that looks unimportant

explanation.direct: The chapter defines collection as moving loose material into capture before deciding what it means.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say partial capture is not enough?
choices: Because collection only works with digital tools
Because uncaptured leftovers keep the mind scanning for what is still outside the system
Because every collected item must become a project

explanation.gentle: Leftover loose items keep attention active.
explanation.direct: Selective capture leaves enough remainder that trust in the system stays weak.
explanation.competitive: Hidden stock keeps security duty alive.

questions.prompt: Which pair best matches what Allen includes in stuff?
choices: Only major goals and calendar appointments
Receipts in pockets and replaying reminders in your head
Reference archives and finished checklists

explanation.gentle: The chapter includes both physical and mental incompletes.
explanation.direct: Stuff is broad: papers, notes, errands, and mental reminders all count when they are still loose.
explanation.competitive: Pocket scraps and replay loops are both inventory.

questions.prompt: Alicia empties her backpack and finds forms, notes, and reminders she had forgotten. What Chapter 5 principle does this show?
choices: A full sweep reveals hidden inventory that was still outside the system
Backpacks should be avoided as capture tools entirely
Only school-related items need to be collected

explanation.gentle: The full sweep makes loose material visible.
explanation.direct: Hidden pockets of incomplete material need to be gathered before the system can be trusted.
explanation.competitive: Dump the cache and the hidden stock finally shows itself.

questions.prompt: What is the trap in opening mail, deciding on each piece, and stopping halfway through the stack?
choices: It makes the mail too easy to find later
It confuses collection with processing and weakens the sweep
It turns all mail into calendar items

explanation.direct: The chapter separates collection from processing so search coverage stays high.

questions.prompt: What failure mode does the chapter warn about in selective capture?
choices: You become too dependent on labels
You may feel a bit better while the structure of distraction stays intact
You stop having any tasks at all

explanation.gentle: Partial relief can hide incomplete gathering.
explanation.direct: Selective collection can improve mood without reducing the unknown remainder enough to build trust.
explanation.competitive: Better feelings are not the same as a secure field.

questions.prompt: A student has loose papers in a locker, reminders in a notebook margin, and one mental promise to email a teacher. What does Chapter 5 suggest?
choices: Collect only the school paper that looks most urgent
Gather the physical and mental incompletes into the same trusted path before deciding anything
Wait until the weekly review and try to remember everything then

explanation.gentle: The chapter broadens collection to include all those loose inputs.
explanation.direct: Physical scraps and replaying reminders belong in the same sweep because both are uncaptured incompletes.

questions.prompt: Someone gathers bills from the counter but leaves receipts in a coat pocket and a form in a bag. How would the chapter judge that?
choices: As enough collection for now because the main stack is handled
As a partial sweep that still leaves the system untrustworthy
As processing rather than collection

explanation.direct: The uncaptured remainder keeps the mind alert because the system has not yet absorbed all loose material.
explanation.competitive: Clear one pile and the side caches still keep the contract.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter link trust in the in-basket to completeness of gathering?
choices: Because the basket is trusted only when loose material has really entered it
Because trust depends on using the same stationery as the author
Because the basket should contain only difficult decisions

explanation.gentle: A tray or list earns trust through use.
explanation.direct: The in-basket becomes credible when side scraps, reminders, and obligations stop living outside it.
explanation.competitive: The basket matters only if it owns the field.

questions.prompt: After a complete collection sweep creates one visible pile, what naturally comes next?
choices: Avoid looking at the pile until motivation improves
Begin processing each item to decide what it is and what should happen
Repeat collection forever without clarifying anything

explanation.gentle: Collection prepares the material for the next stage.
explanation.direct: Once loose inputs are centralized, processing can start taking each item down to empty.
explanation.competitive: After the sweep, every item faces judgment.
